full_judgment:
3. The petitioner has tried to explain the delay in paragraph Nos. 3-5 of his application under section 5 of the Limitation Act. 

 4. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the accused petitioner, submits that in view of the fact that there is no prescribed period of limitation either in the Code of Criminal Procedure or in the Limitation Act for filling a revision, before this Court, the Court usually takes a lenient view in considering the question of delay in such a case. The learned Advocate further submits that the delay involved in the case being due to circumstances beyond the control of the petitioner preventing him from filing the revision case earlier, it is necessary in the interest of justice to condone the seemingly long delay in filing the revision. 

 5. There is no dispute to the fact that neither the Code of Criminal Procedure nor the Limitation Act, 1908 prescribes any period of limitation for filing a revisional application under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but following the long standing practice, which has by now practically become a rule of law, this Court regards 60 days as the period of limitation for filing a criminal revision as provided under Article 155 of the First Schedule of the Limitation Act for a criminal appeal. In spite of this usual practice, nothing prevents this Court from entertaining a revisional application filed beyond 60 days whenever the applicant can satisfy the Court that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from filing the revision earlier or there was any justifiable and acceptable ground for his coming late. The judicial discretion to be exercised by the Court in condoning any justifiable delay is never circumscribed by any rule of law or established judicial principle, the supreme consideration in the whole scheme of the different Codes of law, being the advancement of the cause of justice and not to frustrate it on any technicality. As a matter of fact, this Court has always condoned any reasonable delay whenever it finds that the applicant is not guilty of deliberate laches and negligence in prosecuting his case. On taking a lenient view in interpreting the expression sufficient cause I find instant support of this view in the case of Md Reazuddin Ahmed vs State and another, reported in 17 8LD (AD), 123 wherein their Lordships laid down the principles regulating the subject.
